scenes.visual: Title card: Neighbours Compare.

scenes.tts: The model says cells compare their signals. How do we know real cells do?
scenes.visual: Two fly maps side by side: the embryo and the notum. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: The model says cells compare their signals. How do we know real cells do?

scenes.tts: By the late nineteen eighties, one thing was clear. Embryos lacking Notch or Delta make too many neural cells.
scenes.caption: By the late 1980s, one thing was clear. Embryos lacking Notch or Delta make too many neural cells.
scenes.visual: A timeline marker at the late 1980s.
scenes.narration: By the late 1980s, one thing was clear. Embryos lacking Notch or Delta make too many neural cells.

scenes.tts: What was not clear was how two neighbours, both carrying the receptor and the ligand, make the choice.
scenes.visual: Two neighbouring cells, each with Delta and Notch, and a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: What was not clear was how two neighbours, both carrying the receptor and the ligand, make the choice.

scenes.tts: Start on the embryo map. Fly embryos lacking Notch or Delta make far too many neuroblasts.
scenes.visual: Notch-null embryo cross-section: the nervous system swollen with neuroblasts.
scenes.narration: Start on the embryo map. Fly embryos lacking Notch or Delta make far too many neuroblasts.

scenes.tts: They also make too little epidermis on their underside.
scenes.visual: The ventral epidermis is thin and patchy.
scenes.narration: They also make too little epidermis on their underside.

scenes.tts: Genes like these are called neurogenic. Without the receptor, no cell can be told, not you.
scenes.visual: Label: neurogenic genes. Notch and Delta.
scenes.narration: Genes like these are called neurogenic. Without the receptor, no cell can be told, not you.

scenes.tts: Now the notum. In nineteen ninety-one, Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson made fly mosaics.
scenes.caption: Now the notum. In 1991, Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson made fly mosaics.
scenes.visual: Name card: Heitzler and Simpson, 1991. A notum with patches of cells in a different colour.
scenes.narration: Now the notum. In 1991, Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson made fly mosaics.

scenes.tts: Patches of mutant cells, or cells with a different level of Notch activity, lay beside normal cells.
scenes.visual: A patch border: mutant cells on one side, normal cells on the other.
scenes.narration: Patches of mutant cells, or cells with a different level of Notch activity, lay beside normal cells.

scenes.tts: Then they asked which cells at the patch borders became precursors.
scenes.visual: Border cells highlighted with question marks.
scenes.narration: Then they asked which cells at the patch borders became precursors.

scenes.tts: Cells mutant for Notch became neural on their own.
scenes.visual: Notch-mutant cells at the border turn neural.
scenes.narration: Cells mutant for Notch became neural on their own.

scenes.tts: Predict. What about cells mutant for Delta, beside normal cells?
scenes.visual: Prompt card: Delta-mutant cells beside normal cells. Neural or not?
scenes.narration: Predict. What about cells mutant for Delta, beside normal cells?

scenes.visual: Hold on the prompt. A small timer icon.

scenes.tts: They did not become neural on their own. They still had Notch, so normal neighbours could still say, not you. Losing the receptor and losing the ligand are not the same.
scenes.visual: Reveal: Delta-mutant cells at the border stay non-neural, beside the neural Notch-mutant cells for comparison.
scenes.narration: They did not become neural on their own. They still had Notch, so normal neighbours could still say, not you. Losing the receptor and losing the ligand are not the same.

scenes.tts: Predict again. A normal cell sits beside cells with less Notch activity than its own. What does it become?
scenes.visual: Prompt card: a normal cell between neighbours with smaller, paler crescents.
scenes.narration: Predict again. A normal cell sits beside cells with less Notch activity than its own. What does it become?

scenes.visual: Hold on the prompt. A small timer icon.

scenes.tts: It became epidermis. Beside cells with more Notch activity than its own, the same cell became a neural precursor.
scenes.visual: Reveal: the middle cell flattens into epidermis. Inset: the same cell between high-Notch neighbours turns neural.
scenes.narration: It became epidermis. Beside cells with more Notch activity than its own, the same cell became a neural precursor.

scenes.tts: In these mosaics, a cell's fate depended on its Notch activity relative to the cells beside it.
scenes.visual: Label: relative Notch activity biases fate in these mosaics. A balance between two crescents.
scenes.narration: In these mosaics, a cell's fate depended on its Notch activity relative to the cells beside it.

scenes.tts: Take the pair from chapter three, and give cell A half the normal Notch.
scenes.visual: The A and B pair; A's crescent half size.
scenes.narration: Take the pair from chapter three, and give cell A half the normal Notch.

scenes.tts: A hears its neighbour less, keeps more proneural factor, and wins. That is the logic of the mosaics, in miniature.
scenes.visual: A glows neural, B becomes epidermis.
scenes.narration: A hears its neighbour less, keeps more proneural factor, and wins. That is the logic of the mosaics, in miniature.

scenes.tts: Heitzler and Simpson argued that the cells compete, and that Notch receives an inhibitory signal from the precursors.
scenes.visual: Two cells pushing on each other. Label: competition.
scenes.narration: Heitzler and Simpson argued that the cells compete, and that Notch receives an inhibitory signal from the precursors.

scenes.tts: That picture of lateral inhibition with feedback was later written as a mathematical model.
scenes.visual: The cells fade into the loop diagram from chapter four.
scenes.narration: That picture of lateral inhibition with feedback was later written as a mathematical model.

scenes.tts: That answers the second puzzle, with one qualification. In a sheet, the loop alone gives spaced winners.
scenes.visual: Puzzle card 2, Who does?, gets a check mark with a small footnote: spacing.
scenes.narration: That answers the second puzzle, with one qualification. In a sheet, the loop alone gives spaced winners.

scenes.tts: Neighbours compare their Notch signals, and the comparison helps decide which cell wins.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: relative Notch activity biases fate.
scenes.narration: Neighbours compare their Notch signals, and the comparison helps decide which cell wins.

scenes.visual: Hold on the takeaway card.
